associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: If the liquid is denser, as in the system ice/water, the result illustrated in the figure is obtained. The diagram illustrates that the two changes of T agree with Le Chatelier's principle. The second change of T is opposite to, but smaller than, the first one, as required by Eq 27. On the other hand, the two changes in P do not agree with the principle. Even though the second change of P is opposite to the first one, it is larger, and dP under equilibrium (D = 0) would be of opposite sign to dP under constant ξ. Evidently, we should not attempt to apply the principle to P unless the disturbance is caused by a change of V. In the present case, it is caused by a change in U. Notice that the dashed line in the figure shows an impossible case because it predicts that the second change in T would be opposite to, but larger than, the initial change. Thus, dT under equilibrium (D = 0) would be of opposite sign to dT under constant ξ, which would disagree with Eq 27. Note that the primary disturbances were represented by the same arrow in the figures in order to emphasize that it does not depend on the difference in density between the solid and the liquid. First, suppose we disturbed the internal, two-phase equilibrium by adding a certain amount of heat to a solid/liquid system under constant volume. Then dU = dQ - PdV = dQ. Thus, we would have increased U by dQ and should ask what would happen to the conjugate potential to U, which is -1 / T according to Eq 21. For small changes of T, we could just as well examine T, which may be more convenient. Before there is time for a phase transformation, T will increase, and due to the volume being kept constant, P will also increase to eliminate the thermal expansion. The slope of the arrow representing the initial disturbance would be dP / dT = α / κ where α and κ are the thermal expansion and isothermal compression coefficients, averaged over the phases present.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Cs-Te phase diagram is shown in the figure. This system is of particular interest since Cs and Te fission products in nuclear reactor technology are causative agents in fuel-cladding chemical interaction and fission product-induced liquid metal embrittlement in nuclear reactors. Liquidus and isothermal transformation data were obtained by DTA. Since neither report included tabular data, points were read off the published phase diagrams. These points are shown in the figure. Supplementary visual observations were made on cooling and heating. For alloys of < 20 at.% Te, measurement of the magnetic susceptibility was used to detect solid-liquid transformation. The data are very sparse, whereas a detailed phase diagram was presented. Both groups agree within 10 deg C on the melting point of Cs2Te. Elsewhere, they differ by as much as 50 deg C. Generally, in the assessed diagram, the data were preferred. Taking into account the problem of supercooling, the observed scatter in the data points, and the disagreement between the two studies, it is estimated that error limits of ± 25 deg C should be placed on much of the assessed diagram in the figure. Similarly, the solubility of Cs in solid (Te) is expected to be very small. On this assumption, the limiting liquidus slope at 100 at.% Te in the figure was calculated and was found to agree with the data. This compound was prepared by direct reaction of the elements. It melts incongruity at 660 deg C, as tentatively shown in the figure. However, thermal arrest points observed near 465 deg C and shown in the figure might indicate that the peritectic is actually at this temperature. These compounds were observed, and incongruent melting at 465 and 408 deg C was postulated. However, attempts to prepare the compounds by direct reaction of the elements at 300 deg C yielded only mixtures of Cs2Te3 and Cs3Te2 according to X-ray analysis. The shape of the liquidus, on the other hand, suggests the presence of at least one peritectic at ~ 400 deg C. In the assessed diagram, the existence of these compounds is indicated as tentative, and the thermal arrests observed at 408 deg C are tentatively associated with the incongruent melting of CsTe. Note that the compound NaTe exists in the Na-Te system, and the compound KTe probably exists in the K-Te system. This compound was prepared by high-temperature reaction (CsN3 + Te or Cs2Te3 + Te) and characterized by single crystal X-ray analysis. It was also prepared by direct combination of the elements, and two phase transitions at ~ 120 and ~ 225 deg C were also detected by high-temperature powder X-ray analysis. It is possible that an invariant temperature of 225± 5 deg C, found from thermal analysis, corresponds to this CsTe4 transition. Pending confirmation, these phase transitions are indicated only tentatively in the figure. The compound CsTe5, rather than CsTe4, was postulated, melting incongruity at 263 deg C. An attempt to prepare it from the elements yielded only a CsTe4 +  Te mixture, according to powder X-ray analysis, and this compound does not appear in the figure. Instead, the peritectic at 263 deg C is associated with the incongruent melting of CsTe4.

The selection of critical temperature at 203.5 deg C seems to be the best compromise among the results of all techniques. It was pointed out that the liquidus line should be slightly modified near the critical region. This was corroborated by findings of more shallow slopes of the liquidus on both sides of the critical point. As can be seen, no temperature dependence on the heat of mixing for the liquid was assumed and calculated monotectic and other miscibility gap points are reproduced within the error of experiments. Various methods were used for the liquidus determination. Thermal analysis was performed on various parts of the diagram. The content of both separating liquids after their equilibration was chemically analyzed. Ga amalgams were oxidized with voltammetric and chronopotentiometric methods to find saturating concentrations. The solubility of Ga in Hg was determined by potentiometric investigations. The electrical resistance of an equimolar mixture near the critical point was measured, and neutron transmission for similar conditions was also measured. The Nb-Pt phase diagram was studied in previous works. The assessed phase diagram of the Nb-Pt system is shown in the figure. The phase boundaries and the reaction temperatures are based primarily on work that investigated the system over the entire composition range in the temperature interval of 1000 to $2400^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ by metallography, electron microprobe, XRD, and thermal analysis of 35 arc-melted alloy samples prepared from $99.6\%$ pure Nb and $99.9\%$ pure Pt. The Nb-rich alloys up to 20 at. $\%$ Pt were given homogenization anneals in a vacuum furnace at $1900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for 3 hours, and the other compositions were annealed at 1600 to $1700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for 6 to 12 hours and quenched at rates of 30 to $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ per second. The compositions and the temperatures in the figure have an accuracy of $\pm 1$ at. $\%$ and $\pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , respectively. 
The melting point work showed that the liquidus on the Pt-rich side of the phase diagram has a maximum near 75 at. $\%$ Pt. It was later confirmed by subsequent work, which made an approximate determination of the liquidus by microscopic examination of the melting point samples with visual estimates of the relative amounts of solid and liquid phases present in each sample. Therefore, the liquidus in the figure is shown by broken lines. 
In a recent investigation on Nb-Pt alloys with compositions ranging between 16 and 32 at.%, undercooling by as much as $585\mathrm{K}$ was reported for liquid alloys. The Nb-Pt alloys of 16 to 18 at.% Pt yielded, on undercooling, a single $\mathrm{Nb}_{3}\mathrm{Pt}$ phase in contrast to the $\alpha \mathrm{Nb}$ and $\mathrm{Nb}_{3}\mathrm{Pt}$ phases expected on the basis of the figure. 
Evidence was found for an equiatomic composition alloy which was identified to possess the AuCd-type (B19) orthorhombic structure. The phase is reported to be hyperstoichiometric and is represented as $\mathrm{Nb}_{1 - x}\mathrm{Pt}_{1 + x}$ . It forms at $1700\pm 10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $\sim 43$ at.% Pt by a eutectic reaction, $\mathrm{L}\leftrightarrow \sigma +\mathrm{Nb}_{1 - x}\mathrm{Pt}_{1 + x}$ , and there is agreement as to the temperature and nature of the reaction. There is no structural data on 50 and 51 at.% Pt alloys at $1700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , so it is not justifiable to anchor the Nb-rich phase boundary of the single-phase field of $\mathrm{Nb}_{1 - x}\mathrm{Pt}_{1 + x}$ at $1700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at $\sim 51.2$ at.% Pt, as seen in previous assessments. Microprobe analysis demonstrated the existence of a phase boundary at $1150^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at 52 at.% Pt and at $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at 51 at.% Pt. The existence of a two-phase field at 49 at.% Pt in the temperature range 1500 to $1700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is consistent with the likely farming out of the single-phase field from 52 at.% Pt at 1150 $^\circ \mathrm{C}$ to $\sim 50$ at.% Pt at $1700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ via 51 at.% Pt at $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Hence the Nb-rich phase boundary at $1700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is shifted to $\sim 50$ at.% Pt. XRD of 53 at.% Pt alloy showed the single phase down to $1600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , but two phases at $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and below, indicating a decomposition that is in contradiction with the microprobe results. In view of insufficient information in the range 1500 to $1700^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and conflicting observations at and below $1500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , the Nb-rich phase boundary all along, and the Pt-rich one below $1600^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ are considered tentative and are shown by dashed lines in the assessed phase diagram. Hence the extent of the phase field of $\mathrm{Nb}_{1 - x}\mathrm{Pt}_{1 + x}$ in the assessed diagram is different from those of previous works. A 50 at.% alloy is a two-phase mixture, hence the lattice parameters determined for this composition are not representative of $\mathrm{Nb}_{1 - x}\mathrm{Pt}_{1 + x}$ . 
The Nb-rich boundary of the homogeneity region of $\mathrm{NbPt}_3$ is substantiated by microprobe results from a 74 at.% alloy whereas on the Pt-rich end no structural information is available about intermediate alloys between 75 and 77.5 at.% Pt, as to whether they are monophasic or biphasic. Hence the Pt-rich phase boundary of $\mathrm{NbPt}_3$ is considered tentative and is drawn accordingly by a dashed line in the figure.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Sb-Se phase diagram is based on the thermodynamic assessment. The equilibrium phases in the system are the liquid, L; the terminal solid solution (Sb); the terminal solid solution (Se); and the intermediate phase Sb_2Se_3. The calculated phase diagram using the ionic model is shown. The slope of the liquidus at the Sb-corner is a feature of the calculated phase diagram. The initial slope depends only on the enthalpy of melting of pure Sb and the number of particles per Se atom, which contribute to the configurational entropy in the dilute solution of Se in liquid Sb (Raoult's law). The assumption of one particle per Se atom is considered more realistic than the assumption of Sb_2Se_3 associates, which corresponds to 1/3 particle per Se atom. A metastable miscibility gap of Se-rich liquidus is predicted by the ionic model. Nevertheless, the observation of phase separation phenomena, either in melt-quenched samples or in thermally cycled vapor-deposited samples, is consistent with the calculated metastable gap in the region between Sb_2Se_3 and Se. Limited data indicate that there is no evidence of phase separation by a spinodal mechanism at x_Se > 0.95, which is consistent with the calculated spinodal boundary. However, their data in the range 0.85 < x_Se < 0.91 indicate phase separation by a spinodal mechanism, which seems to be consistent with the calculated spinodal boundary using the ionic model. A systematic study of phase separation, in the range of 60 to 100 at.% Se, in undercooled liquids would be very helpful in discussing the thermodynamics of the Sb-Se liquid. It is worthwhile to mention that a few earlier attempts were made to calculate the Sb-Se phase diagram but only in a limited composition range, and the thermodynamic assessment was the first to calculate the whole phase diagram. Earlier work described the liquid phase in terms of Se_8 rings, Se_4 chains, and Sb_2Se_3 species, and was able to calculate only the Sb_2Se_3-Se part of the phase diagram. Neither earlier work showed the calculated metastable liquid immiscibility. Also, since these authors applied their models only to a part of the phase diagram, it is difficult to make any direct comparison between the earlier calculations and the present assessment.

All stoichiometries, except $\mathrm{Ni}_{11}\mathrm{Zr}_{9}$ and the simple stoichiometries, are based on X-ray diffraction determinations of crystal structures with single crystals. All stoichiometries and crystal structures have been corroborated by at least two investigations. A phase that was reported at $\mathrm{Ni}_{2}\mathrm{Zr}$ with the cubic Laves structure is believed to be due to Si contamination and is not included in the diagram. Input data for the figure show some scatter, but values for invariant temperatures are generally within 10 to $15\mathrm{K}$ of values in the figure. Thermodynamic data for the solid phases are sparse and consist of two sets of measurements. One set involved reaction calorimetric determinations of the enthalpies of formation of four intermediate phases and produced values in $\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{g}$ -atom of: -36.8 for $\mathrm{NiZr}_2$ at $1230\mathrm{K}$ ; -51.5 for $\mathrm{NiZr}$ at $1405\mathrm{K}$ ; -39.5 for $\mathrm{Ni}_7\mathrm{Zr}_2$ at $1670\mathrm{K}$ ; and -32.4 for $\mathrm{Ni}_5\mathrm{Zr}$ at $1479\mathrm{K}$ . The values refer to fcc Ni and bcc Zr as reference states. The other set involved determinations of the Gibbs energies of formation of both crystalline and amorphous material near 36 at.% Zr and of the crystalline phases $\mathrm{Ni}_{10}\mathrm{Zr}_7$ and $\mathrm{Ni}_5\mathrm{Zr}_2$ ( $\mathrm{Ni}_{21}\mathrm{Zr}_8$ in the figure). The determinations were based on measurements of hydrogen vapor pressure isotherms as functions of composition. Enthalpies of formation were derived from the temperature dependences of the Gibbs energies, and values in $\mathrm{kJ} / \mathrm{g}$ -atom were reported as $-48 \pm 4$ for $\mathrm{Ni}_{10}\mathrm{Zr}_7$ and as $-45 \pm 4$ for $\mathrm{Ni}_5\mathrm{Zr}_2$ ( $\mathrm{Ni}_{21}\mathrm{Zr}_8$ ) both through the temperature range 333 to $533\mathrm{K}$ . Since the enthalpies from the vapor pressure data are from limited temperature ranges, these data are less reliable than the calorimetric values. Further, the vapor pressure values refer to fcc Ni and cph Zr rather than to fcc Ni and bcc Zr. In view of these factors, the vapor pressure data accord satisfactorily with the calorimetric data, and the neglect of the vapor pressure results in the calculations is not serious.

associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: The assessed Bi-Cs phase diagram contains original liquidus data points. These points are taken from small diagrams because neither provided tables of data. However, at elevated temperatures and at higher Cs contents, Cs losses by evaporation in the open crucibles could have caused errors. Hence, near the congruent melting point of $\mathrm{BiCs}_3$, the results are considered more accurate. At $>75$ at.% Cs, the liquidus is shown tentatively as having an S-shape, because such behavior is observed in the similar Bi-Na, Bi-K, and Bi-Rb systems. Furthermore, in these three systems, the solubility of Bi in liquid alkali metal is $\sim 1$ at.% at $400^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , dropping to $< 1$ ppm near the melting point of the alkali. A similarly low solubility, therefore, is proposed. From thermal analysis results, a Bi-rich eutectic was proposed at 2.5 at.% Cs at $270^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , whereas it was reported at $250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ at $\sim 3$ at.% Cs in another study. Assuming negligible solid solubility, the limiting slope of the Bi liquidus was calculated thermodynamically from the enthalpy of fusion of Bi as 2.15 degrees per atomic percent Cs. Hence, a eutectic temperature of $270^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ as proposed, involving a freezing point depression of $1.44^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , corresponds to a eutectic composition of 0.7 at.% Cs, which does not lie close to the extrapolated liquidus line. The eutectic temperature of $250^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , reported in another study, corresponds to a eutectic composition of 10 at.% Cs. A eutectic composition of 2 at.% Cs lies on the extrapolated liquidus line, corresponding to a freezing point depression of $3.5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ . Therefore, the eutectic temperature is placed at $267^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , which is within the error limits of the experimental data. This eutectic composition and temperature are also nearly identical to those in the similar Bi-K and Bi-Rb systems. From thermal analysis, an invariant reaction was reported at $501^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , which was associated with the peritectic melting of $\mathrm{Bi}_2\mathrm{Cs}_3$ . Another study reported an invariant at $490^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ , which was tentatively proposed as the peritectic associated with $\mathrm{BiCs}_2$ . An Xray powder pattern of this compound was obtained. Although it could not be indexed, it resembled the powder pattern of the compound $\mathrm{Bi}_2\mathrm{Rb}_3$ , which melts congruently near the 2:3 composition. Hence, the stoichiometry $\mathrm{Bi}_2\mathrm{Cs}_3$ is preferred to $\mathrm{BiCs}_2$ . This compound is shown as melting incongruently. However, within the experimental error limits, congruent melting near $500^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is equally probable. The S-shape in the liquidus at $>75$ at.% Cs, proposed from analogy with the Bi-Na, Bi-K, and Bi-Rb systems, may result from a tendency to immiscibility between liquid Cs and the partially-ionic "liquid compound," $\mathrm{BiCs}_3$ .

The general Schreinemakers' rule states that, at any point, either the boundaries of the N-phase field both must pass into the $(\mathbf{N} + 2)$ -phase field as at points $b$ and $i$ in the figure, or they both must pass into the $(\mathbf{N} + 1)$ -phase fields as at points $c$ , $n$ , and $s$ . In the figure, consider point $A$ , which is in the four-phase region arbitrarily close to point $b$ , and at which $(\gamma + MC)$ is the metastable phase assemblage if precipitation of $\alpha$ is prohibited. It follows that:

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial n _ {\alpha}} \left(\frac {\partial G ^ {(\gamma + M C)}}{\partial n _ {M _ {7} C _ {3}}}\right) <   0 \tag {Eq.5}
$$

where $G(\gamma + MC)$ represents the Gibbs energy of an equilibrium mixture of $\gamma$ and $MC$ phases (alone), where Eq 5 applies at the overall composition of point $b$ , and where $\partial n_{\alpha}$ and $\partial n_{M_{\gamma}C_{3}}$ represent transfers of material with overall compositions of the $\alpha$ and $M_7C_3$ phases, which are at equilibrium with the $(\gamma + MC)$ mixture at point $b$ . associative_matching_result.two_stage_llm_integration: Figure 1 shows the recently reviewed Ca-Zn phase diagram. It features several characteristics that make it a good test case for assessing the effect of differing solution models on the predicted Delta_fG^0 values for intermetallic compounds. These include: (a) a binary compound (CaZn_2) with a negligible solid solution range, in equilibrium with a solution (the liquid) over a wide temperature range; (b) noncontroversial (or at least uncontradicted) liquidus compositions, in this case those reported; and (c) a single reliable set of data for the thermodynamic properties of liquid alloys as a function of composition and temperature, specifically the vapor-pressure measurements. The assumptions of a stoichiometric compound, accurate phase-boundary compositions, and reliable solution thermodynamic data are the other possible sources of error that will be assessed later.
